name: Land grants to Brahmins, temples and officials
what: Copper-plate grants handed villages, their revenue and often their policing to Brahmins, temples and later officials.

name: Age of regional kingdoms in India
what: After Harsha no power ruled the whole north; Pratiharas, Palas, Rashtrakutas and Cholas built strong regional states instead.

name: Tripartite struggle for Kanauj
what: Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas fought for 150 years over the old imperial city of Kanauj without any of them keeping it.

name: Monsoon-fed nuclear regions of power
what: Rice deltas and river valleys separated by forest, hills and dry plateau formed separate agrarian cores, each able to feed a kingdom.

name: Armed peasantry and the military labour market
what: Millions of peasants owned weapons and sold their service to whoever paid, so soldiers were cheap for any challenger to hire.

name: Arid-zone frontier and the horse trade
what: India bred poor warhorses; the dry belt from Sind to the Deccan and the imports from Central Asia decided who had cavalry.

name: Mahmud of Ghazni raids India
what: Some seventeen raids from Ghazni plundered temple cities from Multan to Somnath.

name: Mongol pressure on the Delhi Sultanate
what: Repeated Mongol invasions forced the sultans to keep a huge standing cavalry army paid from centralised revenue.

name: Muhammad bin Tughluq overreaches and the south breaks away
what: Moving the capital to Daulatabad and taxing the Doab hard, the sultan lost the Deccan to the Bahmanis and Vijayanagara.

name: Breakaway sultanates after Firuz Shah
what: Governors of Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, Jaunpur and the Deccan made themselves kings; Babur found five sultans and two rajas.

name: Persianate revenue state: cash land tax and assignments
what: Delhi and its heirs assessed land in cash and paid soldiers with revocable revenue assignments (iqta, later jagir).

name: Chola temple-centred redistribution
what: Kings endowed great temples that pooled land, gold and labour, binding local peasant assemblies to the dynasty by gift.

name: Chola naval raid on Srivijaya
what: Rajendra I sent a fleet that sacked Srivijaya's ports across the Strait of Malacca.

name: The Sanskrit cosmopolis
what: One courtly language and model of kingship spread from Afghanistan to Java without any empire behind it.

name: Nayaka military lordships of Vijayanagara
what: Vijayanagara kings granted territories to warrior chiefs (nayakas) who kept armies and later founded their own kingdoms.

name: Akbar's mansabdari-jagirdari system
what: Ranked officers (mansabdars) held rotating jagirs to pay their troops, so no noble put down roots in one province.

name: Mughal-Rajput alliance
what: Marriage and high rank tied the Rajput clans to the throne from Akbar's Amber match in 1562.

name: The Mughal empire at its greatest extent
what: With Bijapur and Golconda taken, the Mughals ruled almost all of the subcontinent and perhaps 150 million people.

name: Heavy revenue demand on the Mughal peasantry
what: The state claimed roughly a third to a half of the harvest, and short-tenure jagirdars squeezed more.

name: Jagirdari crisis
what: More nobles than paying jagirs: the Deccan wars inflated the nobility while revenue-yielding land lagged.

name: Jat, Satnami, Sikh and zamindar revolts
what: Peasant and gentry risings around Agra, Mathura and the Punjab defied Mughal revenue collection.

name: Aurangzeb's Deccan wars
what: Aurangzeb spent his last 26 years in the south conquering Bijapur and Golconda and chasing the Marathas.

name: Maratha expansion
what: Maratha armies collected chauth and sardeshmukhi across the Deccan, Gujarat, Malwa and into Bengal and the Punjab.

name: Mughal succession wars after Aurangzeb
what: Five emperors in twelve years; court factions made and unmade rulers.

name: Successor states: Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad
what: Mughal governors kept Mughal forms and revenue machinery but made their provinces hereditary kingdoms.

name: Bankers, revenue farmers and portfolio capitalists
what: Banking houses like the Jagat Seths and revenue farmers financed regional rulers and later the East India Company.

name: The Company takes the diwani of Bengal
what: By the Treaty of Allahabad the Mughal emperor granted the East India Company the revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

name: Company military-fiscal state in India
what: Land revenue paid sepoy armies that won more land: a war machine that conquered India by 1818.

name: Indian cotton cloth dominates world markets
what: Gujarat, Coromandel and Bengal weavers clothed Africa, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and, via the companies, Europe.

name: British Calico Acts ban Indian printed cottons
what: Parliament banned Indian printed calicoes (1700) and their wearing (1721), sheltering British imitators.

name: Mechanisation of British cotton spinning
what: Jenny, water frame and mule cut the labour in a pound of yarn by more than ninety per cent.

name: Rising grain prices and wages in 18th-century India
what: Political disorder and droughts drove up grain prices, raising the nominal wage weavers needed and eroding their price edge.

name: The great El Nino of 1789-93
what: Failed monsoons and the Doji Bara famine in south and west India, part of a global drought.

name: Collapse of Indian handloom exports and domestic share
what: India went from exporting cloth to importing Lancashire yarn and cloth; spinning, mostly women's work, collapsed first.

name: Charter Act ends the Company's India trade monopoly
what: Opened India to private British traders and Manchester goods.

name: Permanent Settlement of Bengal
what: Cornwallis fixed the land revenue forever and made zamindars owners of the soil.

name: Home charges and the drain
what: India paid London for debt, pensions, the India Office and the army, financed by an export surplus: the "drain".

name: Drain theory becomes Indian economic nationalism
what: Naoroji, Ranade and Dutt argued British rule impoverished India by draining its surplus abroad.

name: Swadeshi movement
what: Boycott of British cloth after the partition of Bengal, the first mass campaign of Indian nationalism.

name: Railways built across India
what: From 1853 to 1930 some 67,000 km of track joined inland districts to ports and to each other.

name: Bombay cotton mill industry
what: Indian capitalists built mechanised mills from 1854; by 1914 India had one of the world's largest cotton industries.

name: Export cash crops: cotton, jute, wheat, indigo, opium
what: Railways and the Suez canal pulled Indian farms into world markets.

name: Punjab canal colonies
what: Perennial canals turned dry doabs into wheat and cotton land settled by millions.

name: Company revenue collection held up through the 1769-70 drought
what: Revenue receipts barely fell as perhaps a third of Bengal's people died.

name: Minimal relief and grain exports in the famine of 1876-78
what: Lytton's government refused to interfere with grain markets and cut relief rations (the Temple wage).

name: Malthusian and laissez-faire famine doctrine
what: Officials schooled in Malthus and Smith held that relief bred dependency and trade would move grain best.

name: Famine Commission and Famine Codes
what: The 1880 Famine Commission led to provincial Famine Codes: relief works, early warning, scarcity declarations.

name: El Nino droughts of 1896-97 and 1899-1900
what: Two of the worst monsoon failures on record within four years.

name: Famine mortality falls after 1908
what: Droughts kept coming but no longer killed millions until 1943.

name: Japan takes Burma and Burmese rice stops
what: Bengal lost the rice imports it had relied on in poor seasons.

name: Denial policy in coastal Bengal
what: Fearing invasion, the authorities seized boats and removed rice from coastal districts.

name: October 1942 cyclone and rice brown spot
what: A cyclone, flooding and fungal disease cut the winter aman crop in western Bengal.

name: Wartime inflation in Bengal
what: Military spending and hoarding drove rice prices up several-fold while rural wages lagged.

name: Collapse of rural labourers' food entitlements
what: Fishermen, labourers and artisans could no longer buy rice; they died in their millions.

name: Epidemic malaria in famine years
what: Most famine deaths came from malaria, cholera and dysentery in starved bodies.

name: Abbasid revolution
what: A movement from Khurasan overthrew the Umayyads; the new dynasty moved the centre of power east to Iraq.

name: Graeco-Arabic translation movement
what: Nearly all of Greek science and philosophy that survived, plus Persian and Indian works, was put into Arabic.

name: Abbasids adopt Sasanian imperial ideology
what: Al-Mansur's court presented the caliphs as heirs of Persian kings who had restored scattered Greek learning.

name: Abbasid Gulf trade with India and China
what: Ships from Basra and Siraf sailed the monsoon to India and Canton.

name: The Mihna (inquisition)
what: Al-Ma'mun made scholars profess the created Quran; its failure left religious authority with the ulama, not the caliph.

name: Turkish guard and the anarchy at Samarra
what: Al-Mu'tasim's slave soldiers made and killed caliphs; four were murdered in nine years (861-870).

name: Zanj rebellion
what: Enslaved East Africans draining the salt marshes near Basra rose and held southern Iraq for fourteen years.

name: Decline of the Sawad irrigation system
what: Canals in central Iraq silted and were abandoned as the state stopped maintaining them; settlement shrank.

name: Buyids take Baghdad
what: Daylamite warlords ruled Iraq in the caliph's name; the caliph kept only his title.

name: Spread of the iqta
what: Unable to pay salaries, rulers assigned tax revenue from land directly to commanders.

name: 11th-century cold spells in Iran and the eastern Mediterranean
what: Harsh winters and droughts hit cotton farming and pushed Turkish nomads south.

name: Seljuks enter Baghdad
what: Tughril Beg took Baghdad as sultan; Sunni Turks replaced the Shi'i Buyids.

name: Nizamiyya madrasas
what: Nizam al-Mulk endowed law colleges to train Sunni jurists and officials.

name: Maragha observatory
what: Hulagu funded al-Tusi's observatory; its astronomers built the non-Ptolemaic models later found in Copernicus.

name: Late flowering of Islamic astronomy and mathematics
what: Ibn al-Shatir in Damascus, Ulugh Beg in Samarkand and al-Kashi kept the field advancing long after the supposed decline.

name: Diffusion of crops across the early Islamic world
what: Rice, sugar cane, cotton and citrus spread west from India and Iran, with summer irrigation.

name: Islamic partnership and inheritance law
what: Partnerships dissolved at a partner's death and estates split among many heirs, so firms stayed small and short-lived.

name: Waqf endowments lock capital
what: Pious trusts held huge assets under founders' fixed terms, hard to redeploy.

name: The Middle East falls behind western Europe economically
what: By 1800 per capita incomes and commercial institutions lagged the North Sea economies.

name: Military slavery in Islamic states
what: Rulers relied on purchased slave soldiers (ghulams, mamluks) rather than landed vassals.

name: Shorter, less stable reigns of Muslim rulers
what: After about 1000, sultans' reigns grew shorter while European kings' grew longer.

name: Ottoman delay in Arabic-script printing
what: Muslims did not print in Arabic script in the empire until Ibrahim Muteferrika's press of 1727.

name: Mongol conquest of Khwarazm and Khurasan
what: Chinggis Khan destroyed the Khwarazmshah and massacred cities from Bukhara to Nishapur.

name: Depopulation of Iraq after 1258
what: Settlement on the Diyala plains fell to its lowest level in millennia.

name: Shadow Abbasid caliphate in Mamluk Cairo
what: The Mamluks installed a surviving Abbasid as caliph to legitimise their sultans.

name: Ilkhanid patronage of science and history
what: Mongol rulers in Tabriz funded Rashid al-Din's world history and Chinese-Persian exchange.

name: High real wages in the Middle East after plagues
what: As after the Justinianic plague, labour scarcity raised urban real wages for a few generations.

name: Classical Ottoman order: timar, devshirme and kul
what: Cavalry paid by timar land grants and a palace slave elite recruited by the boy levy.

name: Price inflation and silver influx in the Ottoman Empire
what: Prices roughly quadrupled in silver terms over a long century as New World silver flowed east.

name: Debasement of the akce
what: The silver coin lost about half its silver; the janissaries revolted in 1589 when paid in it.

name: From timariot cavalry to musket infantry
what: Habsburg wars demanded musketeers; the janissary corps grew and cash taxes replaced timars.

name: Great drought and cold in Anatolia
what: The worst drought in six centuries of tree-ring record, during the Little Ice Age's coldest phase.

name: Celali revolts
what: Unpaid mercenaries and desperate peasants ravaged Anatolia; villages emptied for a generation.

name: Regicide of Osman II
what: Janissaries and ulama deposed and killed a sultan who planned to replace them.

name: The "Second Empire": jurists and janissaries constrain the sultan
what: Power shifted from the dynasty to a broad political class that limited royal absolutism.

name: Life-term tax farms (malikane)
what: Tax sources were sold for life for a large down payment, creating a class of investor-officials.

name: Rise of provincial notables (ayan)
what: Local magnates ran provinces and armies under nominal Ottoman sovereignty.

name: Treaty of Karlowitz
what: The first great Ottoman cession: Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs.

name: Russo-Ottoman war and Kuchuk Kainardji
what: Defeat by Russia lost the Crimea's protection and opened the Black Sea.

name: Destruction of the janissaries
what: Mahmud II massacred the corps and built a new army.

name: Anglo-Ottoman commercial treaty of Balta Limani
what: Low tariffs and no monopolies opened Ottoman markets to British goods.

name: Ottoman manufacturing adapts
what: Rural, female and small-shop production, carpets and silk kept manufacturing alive against British imports.

name: Ottoman default and the Public Debt Administration
what: After two decades of foreign borrowing the state defaulted; European creditors took over key revenues.

name: Ottoman "decline" advice literature
what: Officials like Mustafa Ali and Koci Bey wrote that the empire had decayed since Suleiman.

name: Southeast Asia's age of commerce
what: Booming trade in spices, pepper and cloth built port cities like Malacca, Aceh, Banten and Makassar.

name: Pepper, clove and nutmeg boom
what: European and Chinese demand multiplied exports from Sumatra, Java and the Moluccas.

name: Islamisation of the archipelago's port states
what: Trading rulers from Malacca to Ternate adopted Islam with the merchant networks.

name: VOC spice monopoly and the conquest of Banda
what: Coen took Batavia and depopulated the Banda Islands (1621) to control nutmeg.

name: Seventeenth-century crisis in maritime Southeast Asia
what: Port states lost trade to the Dutch, prices fell, and rulers turned inland and absolutist.

name: Drier 17th century in Southeast Asia
what: Tree rings show weaker monsoons in the 1600s.

name: Mainland consolidation: Burma, Siam and Vietnam
what: Over centuries dozens of mainland polities fused into three, in parallel with France, Russia and Japan.

name: Firearms and Portuguese gunners in mainland warfare
what: Toungoo Burma used maritime wealth to buy guns and mercenaries.

name: Angkor's water management network
what: Barays, canals and embankments over 1,000 km2 of low-density city redistributed monsoon water.

name: Extreme monsoon floods at Angkor
what: Very wet years between the droughts sent erosive floods through the canals.

name: Breakdown of Angkor's water network
what: Erosion, silting and breached embankments cascaded through the interlinked system.

name: Gradual depopulation of Angkor's core
what: Urban activity in Angkor Thom's moat and around Angkor Wat dwindled from the 14th century, not in one blow.

name: Khmer capital shifts south to the river trade
what: Kings moved to the Phnom Penh area, where the Mekong carried Chinese and maritime trade.

name: Theravada Buddhism replaces the Angkorian state cult
what: A monk-centred popular Buddhism needed no vast royal temples.

name: Angkor at its height
what: Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom built; the urban complex held perhaps 700,000-900,000 people.

name: European "rediscovery" of Angkor
what: Mouhot's posthumous book made Angkor a "lost city" in Europe, though Cambodians had never left it.

name: Trade shifts from the Gulf to the Red Sea
what: Fatimid Cairo and Aden captured the India trade as Iraq declined.

name: Geniza merchants' India trade
what: Jewish traders from Cairo and Aden ran partnerships with Malabar ports, recorded in the Cairo Geniza.

name: Portuguese cartaz system
what: Asian ships had to buy Portuguese passes and call at Portuguese forts or be seized.

name: Asian merchants keep most Indian Ocean trade
what: Gujarati, Chulia, Arab, Persian and Malay shippers carried the bulk of the ocean's trade until the 18th century.

name: Revival of the Red Sea spice route
what: By the 1560s Venice was again buying as much pepper in Alexandria as before da Gama.

name: English and Dutch East India Companies founded
what: Joint-stock companies with charters to trade, fight and govern east of the Cape.

name: American silver flows into Mughal India
what: Europeans paid for Indian cloth and pepper mostly in silver; Mughal mints coined it into rupees.

name: Cash land revenue and the monetised Mughal economy
what: Revenue assessed and paid in silver pushed peasants to sell crops and drew money into the countryside.

name: Decline of Surat's merchant shipping
what: Surat's Muslim shipowners lost their Red Sea and Gulf markets as Mughal, Safavid and Ottoman hinterlands faltered.

name: Decline of towns and long-distance trade in early medieval India (contested)
what: R.S. Sharma read fewer coins and shrinking urban layers as a collapse of trade after the Guptas; others see relocation, not decline.

name: Ritual sovereignty over self-governing localities
what: In Stein's model the Chola king ruled his core directly but held the peripheral nadus only by ritual precedence.

name: Caste order separates status from power
what: Brahmins ranked above kings; castes and villages governed much of daily life on their own.

name: Company paramountcy after the last Maratha war
what: Defeat of the Peshwa left the East India Company sovereign or suzerain over almost all of India.

name: Regional economic growth in Awadh, Bengal and the Punjab
what: Zamindars, merchants and small towns prospered as wealth moved from the imperial centre to the provinces.

name: Ruralisation: more Indians depend on farming
what: The share of Indian workers in industry fell as spinners and weavers turned to the land.

name: India's export surplus settles Britain's deficits
what: India's trade surplus with the rest of the world paid its deficit with Britain, closing Britain's global balance.

name: Failure of the 1769 rains in Bengal
what: The monsoon failed after a poor 1768 harvest.

name: War Cabinet limits grain shipments to India
what: London refused or delayed most requests for wheat imports to India in 1943 to save shipping.

name: Religious authority passes to the ulama
what: After the Mihna failed, scholars, not caliphs, defined the faith and lent rulers their legitimacy.

name: Decline of Nishapur and Iran's cotton economy
what: The great cotton city shrank amid cold, famine and Turkmen raids.

name: Slowdown of Arabic natural science (contested)
what: Whether, when and why innovative science in Arabic slowed is the core of the debate.

name: The Great Flight from the Anatolian countryside
what: Peasants fled Celali bands and famine for towns and the Balkans; thousands of villages emptied.

name: The state co-opts bandit leaders with offices
what: Istanbul bought off Celali chiefs with governorships, turning rebels into servants.

name: Ottoman armies fall behind their European rivals
what: From Vienna to the Russian wars, Ottoman forces lost more battles than they won.

name: Forest clearance and erosion in Angkor's catchment
what: Clearing the uplands for rice and building sent sediment into the canals.

name: Tax-free religious endowments at Pagan
what: Kings and nobles gave vast tax-exempt lands and labour to the sangha.

name: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
what: The first Portuguese fleet to reach India by the Cape anchored off Calicut in May 1498.

sources.cite: A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497-1499 1898

name: Decline of the overland Levant spice caravans
what: By the 1630s pepper and spices to Europe went round the Cape in company ships, not across the Middle East.

name: European shipping dominates Indian Ocean trade
what: British private traders and the Company took over the routes once run by Surat and Masulipatnam.

name: Jahangir
what: Mughal emperor 1605-1627, author of the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.

name: H.G. Keene
what: Henry George Keene, British Indian civil servant and historian of the late Mughals.

name: James Talboys Wheeler
what: British historian of India and official in the Government of India.

name: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq
what: Flemish diplomat, Habsburg ambassador to Suleiman the Magnificent, author of the Turkish Letters.

name: Alvaro Velho (attributed)
what: Sailor on Vasco da Gama's first voyage, the usual attribution of the anonymous Roteiro.

name: Duarte Barbosa
what: Portuguese scrivener in Kerala, author of a description of the Indian Ocean coasts c. 1516.

name: Henri Mouhot
what: French naturalist whose posthumous travels popularised Angkor in Europe.
